deep.reconstruction:
The page holds two unrelated blocks of material.

(A) MAIN TEXT: 'Nova theorematis pythagoraei demonstratio' (a new proof of the Pythagorean theorem).

Theorem: in triangle ABC with a right angle at A, AB^2 + AC^2 = BC^2.

Proof as written:
1. Produce AB both ways to D (beyond A) and F (beyond B), with BD = BF = BC. The collinear order is D, A, B, F.
2. Triangles CBD and CBF are isosceles, so angle BDC = angle BCD and angle BCF = angle BFC.
3. Gauss asserts BDC + DCB + BCF + CFB = 2 right angles. My justification: the angle sums of the two triangles give 4R, less CBD + CBF = 2R (supplementary angles at B), leaving 2R.
4. With the equalities of step 2 this gives 2(DCB + BCF) = 2R. So angle DCF = DCB + BCF = R. This is Thales: C lies on the circle with centre B and diameter DF.
5. Hence angle CDA = angle ACF. My justification: in right triangle ACD, CDA = R - ACD, and ACF = DCF - DCA = R - ACD. So triangles ACD and AFC (both right-angled at A) are similar.
6. Therefore AC : AD = AF : AC, so AC^2 = AD·AF, the rectangle under AD and AF.
7. AD = BD - AB = BC - AB and AF = AB + BF = AB + BC. So AC^2 = (BC - AB)(BC + AB), which equals BC^2 - AB^2 by Euclid Elements II (II.5/II.6).
8. Hence AC^2 + AB^2 = BC^2. QED.

In modern terms this is the mean-proportional (altitude/intersecting-chord) property h^2 = (c-b)(c+b) in the circle of radius c centred at B.

(B) MARGINAL SCRIBBLES: series on the lemniscatic functions, read from the image.
- Upper line (with a partly struck first attempt above it): x + (1/2)(1/5)x^5 + (1/2)(3/4)(1/9)x^9 + ...
  This is the binomial expansion of the lemniscatic arc integral ∫_0^x dt/sqrt(1-t^4) = x + x^5/10 + x^9/24 + ...
- Next line: x - (1/10)x^5 + (1/120)x^9 ...
  This is the reversed series, i.e. the lemniscatic sine sl(x) = x - x^5/10 + x^9/120 - ...
- Next: (ϖ/π)(s + (1/2)(1/3)s^3 + (1·3)/(2·4·5)s^5 ...), i.e. (ϖ/π)·arcsin s, with some struck terms.
- Then: (ϖ/π)s + (1/6)(ϖ/π)s^3 + (3/40)(ϖ/π)s^5 ... - (1/10)(ϖ/π)^5 (s^5).
  This is the start of the expansion of sl((ϖ/π) arcsin s) in powers of s = sin φ. Here ϖ = 2∫_0^1 dt/sqrt(1-t^4) ≈ 2.62206 is Gauss's lemniscate constant. The aim is evidently to compare the lemniscatic sine of the argument ϖφ/π with sin φ, i.e. to study sl(ϖφ/π) as a function of φ.
- A lone ϖ/π also stands under the theorem.
- Around the first triangle sketch are formulas written in mirror script. Read reversed, they appear to involve ∫ φ sin φ dφ, φ cos φ and sin^2 φ type terms, plausibly an integration by parts such as ∫ φ sin φ dφ = -φ cos φ + sin φ. This reading is tentative.

The next page holds unrelated long decimal multiplications (e.g. 1190.25^n, 2380.5^2 = 5666780.25? partial products 157410.5625 = 396.75^2 etc.).
errors: No mathematical error in the proof. Step 3 (the four angles summing to two right angles) is asserted without stating the reason: angle sums of the two triangles minus the straight angle at B.
The figure places D beyond A, so AD = BC - AB requires BC > AB. This holds automatically because BC is the hypotenuse; it is unstated but harmless.

Marginal series check out as far as written: arcsin coefficients 1/6, 3/40; lemniscatic integral 1/10, 1/24; sl coefficients -1/10, 1/120; composition term -(ϖ/π)^5 s^5/10. The expansion is truncated, so the s^5 coefficient is complete but higher terms are not given.

results.what: Proof of Pythagoras: extend AB so that BD = BF = BC, show angle DCF is right (Thales), derive AC^2 = AD·AF = (BC-AB)(BC+AB) from similar triangles
results.modern_name: Pythagorean theorem via mean proportional / intersecting chords (circle centred at B of radius BC)
results.usually_credited_to: Classical; essentially Euclid III.35/VI.13 with II.5. Variants are listed in Loomis, The Pythagorean Proposition (1927/1940), and the idea is old (medieval/early-modern)

results.what: Series ∫_0^x dt/sqrt(1-t^4) = x + x^5/10 + x^9/24 + ... and its inversion sl x = x - x^5/10 + x^9/120 - ...
results.modern_name: Taylor series of the lemniscatic arc integral and of the lemniscatic sine
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (1797, Tagebuch and lemniscate papers, Werke III/X); Fagnano and Euler for the integral

results.what: Expansion of sl((ϖ/π) arcsin s) = (ϖ/π)s + (ϖ/π)s^3/6 + (3/40)(ϖ/π)s^5 - (ϖ/π)^5 s^5/10 + ...
results.modern_name: Composition of lemniscatic sine with scaled arcsine (comparison of sl(ϖφ/π) with sin φ)

deep.surprise_reason: The Pythagorean proof is a known classical variant built on the mean-proportional/Thales argument. The marginal lemniscatic series and the constant ϖ are well-documented Gauss material from 1797 onward. The page is of biographical interest (an early juvenile exercise beside lemniscate scratch work) but contains nothing new.

x - x^5/10 + x^9/120 inverts the arc series to O(x^13), giving the lemniscatic sine coefficients
expansion of sl((ϖ/π) arcsin s) through s^5 with k = ϖ/π

transcription_corrections: The upper series line reads x + (1/2)(1/5)x^5 + (1/2)(3/4)(1/9)x^9 ..., i.e. powers 5 and 9 with denominators 5 and 9. It is not the arcsin series with x^3, x^5.
The second series line reads x - (1/10)x^5 + (1/120)x^9 ..., the lemniscatic sine. It is not x - x^3/6 + x^5/120 (sine).
The last marginal term is -(1/10)(ϖ/π)^5 (times s^5), not -(1/6)(ϖ/π)^3.
The struck line at the left margin is an earlier attempt at the same lemniscatic series (it shows a 5 in a denominator and x^5), not the arcsin series.

The 'cipher-like scribbles' around the upper triangle appear to be mirror-written formulas with φ, sin φ, cos φ and integral signs (e.g. ∫ φ sin φ dφ ...). They are not illegible cipher, though the exact reading is uncertain.
In the main proof, the struck word before 'CDA' and the struck word in 'Rctg. ... sub AD et AF' are cancellations, consistent with the transcription.
